food.text: Around 4500 BC a Neolithic package of cereal cultivars, housing and stone monuments arrived in Ireland. Sheep, goats, cattle and cereals were imported from southwestern continental Europe, after which the population rose significantly.
In Cornwall, the first evidence for domesticated crops dates to c. 4000 BCE. After 4000 BCE, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, wheat and barley were introduced into Southern Britain from Europe.
Archaeological evidence of cheese production in Britain can be seen as early as 3,800 BC. Bread from cereal grains was being produced as early as 3,700 BC.

In France, the first farmers appeared in the Neolithic, which began in the south in the middle of the 6th millennium BC. Neolithic groups subsisted on domestic plants and animals, supplemented with collected wild plant foods and hunting.

After 4000 BCE, domesticated animals such as cattle, pigs, sheep, and goats, along with cereals like wheat and barley, were introduced into Southern Britain from Europe. The first evidence for domesticated crops in Cornwall dates to c. 4000 BCE.

The earliest clear proof of farmers in Ireland or Great Britain comes from Ferriter's Cove on the Dingle Peninsula. There, a flint knife, cattle bones and a sheep's tooth were found and dated to c. 4350 BC.

At the Céide Fields in County Mayo, an extensive Neolithic field system, arguably the oldest known in the world, has been preserved beneath a blanket of peat. Small fields were separated by dry-stone walls and farmed for several centuries between 3500 and 3000 BC.

The Mesolithic Irish were hunter-gatherers whose settlements lay close to water systems. This suggests a diet rich in vegetation, marine life and smaller mammals, unlike their British contemporaries, whose settlements further inland favoured a diet with more meat.
The main crops grown at the Céide Fields were wheat and barley. Pottery appeared around the same time as agriculture, and typical ware included wide-mouthed, round-bottomed bowls.
Irish bogs have preserved organic materials exceptionally well because of their anaerobic conditions. Among the finds is a Mesolithic wicker fish-trap, a rare glimpse of how early people caught food.

Ancient DNA studies suggest that agriculture was introduced to Britain by migrating Early European Farmer groups bringing their Neolithic lifestyle from the European mainland. This argues against the idea that indigenous British hunter-gatherers became farmers themselves.

Because Ireland's acidic soils have long since decomposed immediate food products, archaeologists rely on byproducts such as bone fragments and sea shells. Deer features minimally in the finds, thought to be due to the infrequent presence of deer along coastal regions, bays and estuaries.

The Chasséen culture, dated 4,500 to 3,500 BC, is named after Chassey-le-Camp in Saône-et-Loire. It spread throughout the plains and plateaux of France, including the Seine basin and the upper Loire valleys, among Neolithic farming communities.

Around 4300 BC cattle arrived in northern Ireland during the late Mesolithic period. The red deer was introduced from Britain at about the same time. Ireland's bogs have also preserved a Mesolithic wicker fish-trap, thanks to anaerobic conditions.

art.text: In France, the first megaliths were erected in the early 5th millennium BC. This came after the first farmers appeared in the south of the country, around the middle of the 6th millennium BC, when the Neolithic began there.

France has some 5,000 megalithic monuments, mainly in Brittany, which holds the largest concentration. Dolmens and menhirs at Carnac and elsewhere begin to appear in the fifth millennium BC, though some authors speculate about Mesolithic roots.

The earliest known architecture in England is the megalithic tombs of the Neolithic, such as Wayland's Smithy and the West Kennet Long Barrow. Radiocarbon dating shows that the earliest of them are nearly 1,500 years older than the first of the pyramids of Egypt.
In the Neolithic, which begins in the south of France in the middle of the 6th millennium BC, the first farmers appeared. The first megaliths were erected in the early 5th millennium BC.
The Cairn of Gavrinis in southern Brittany is an outstanding example of megalithic art. Its 14 meter inner corridor is nearly completely adorned with ornamental carvings.

Neolithic farming brought permanent settlements to Scotland, like the stone house at Knap of Howar on Papa Westray, from around 3500 BCE. Settlers also introduced chambered cairn tombs, as at Maeshowe, and standing stones and circles such as those at Stenness on Orkney, dating from about 3100 BCE.
Among the figurines from Links of Noltland is the Westray Wife. It is the earliest known depiction of a human face from Scotland, and it dates from the Neolithic period.

Around 4000 BC, constructions were being built in Brittany (Carnac), central and southern France, England, Wales and Northern Ireland (Banbridge), among other places. By c. 3000 BC the first henges, which are circular earthworks, had appeared in Britain.

The earliest portable art from what is now Scotland is highly decorated carved stone balls from the Neolithic period. Their patterns are shared with Irish and Scottish stone carvings. Elaborate carved maceheads also survive from this period.

The Grand-Pressigny area of France was known for its precious silex blades, which were extensively exported during the Neolithic. France also has numerous painted stones, polished stone axes and inscribed menhirs from this period.

science.text: The bow and arrow was known in Western Europe since at least 9000 BC. Hunting in Mesolithic England was mainly done with simple projectile weapons such as the javelin and possibly the sling.

Many areas of Europe entered the Neolithic with a package of cereal cultivars, pastoral animals, pottery, weaving, housing and burial cultures, all arriving together. The package began in central Europe as LBK about 6000 BC, and within several hundred years this culture was present in northern France.

The Mesolithic period in Cornwall, from c. 10,000 to 4000 BCE, was marked by advances in stone tool technology. These allowed hunter-gatherers to exploit the newly formed woodland environment and additional marine and freshwater resources that came with the warmer temperatures and rising sea levels of the Holocene.

The first ceramics in Cornwall date to c. 4000 BCE, in the style known as Hembury Ware. Most of it was made using gabbroic clay from the Lizard, and the vessels could have been prestige items crafted by specialist potters and traded across southern Britain.

By 5100 BC there is evidence of dairy practices in southern England. Modern English cattle appear to be derived from "T1 Taurids" that were domesticated in the Aegean region shortly after the onset of the Holocene.

Around 6200 BCE, a tsunami from the Storegga Slide, a submarine landslide off the coast of Norway, may have flooded much of Doggerland's remaining coastal land, with a catastrophic impact on the Mesolithic people living on the coast. It is estimated that up to a quarter of the Mesolithic population of Britain lost their lives. A 2014 study suggested the only parts of Doggerland left at the time were low-lying islands, but supported the view that the area was abandoned at about the same time as the tsunamis.

Mesolithic people in England were manipulating their environment and prey in new ways. The evidence suggests possible selective burning of the then-omnipresent woodland to create clearings where herds would gather and be hunted.

Carinated Bowls are infrequent finds in Cornwall, yet they appear in unusually large numbers at Carn Brea. There they were made from gabbroic fabric, while at a few other sites they were made from a blend of gabbroic and local clays.

The La Hoguette culture arrived in France's northwestern region and appears to derive from the Ibero Italian-Eastern Adriatic Impressed Cardial Ware culture (Cardium pottery). Like the western Cardial culture, it raised sheep and goats more intensely.

politics.text: Near Carnac in Brittany, the tumulus of Saint-Michel was built as a tomb for members of the ruling class. It measures 125 by 60 metres at its base, stands 12 metres high, and took 35,000 cubic metres of stone and earth to build. It was constructed between 5000 BCE and 3400 BCE.

When farmers arrived in Britain, the island was inhabited by hunter-gatherer groups, the first inhabitants since the last Ice Age ended about 11,700 years ago. The farmers replaced most of the hunter-gatherer population in the British Isles without mixing much with them.

The Sweet Track, a timber causeway in the Somerset Levels, was built in 3807 BC and stretched about 1,800 metres between an island at Westhay and high ground at Shapwick. It was one of a network of tracks that once crossed the Levels. It was used for only around ten years before being abandoned, probably because of rising water.

Newgrange in County Meath, Ireland, is a grand passage tomb built around 3100 BC, making it older than Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids. Some of its material came from as far as the Mournes and Wicklow Mountains. It is the main monument of the Brú na Bóinne complex, which also includes Knowth and Dowth.

The Céide Fields in County Mayo, Ireland, hide more than 100 km of stone field walls beneath blanket bog. The site is traditionally interpreted as a Neolithic farming landscape of the fourth millennium BCE. Andrew Whitefield has suggested it may be more comparable to later Bronze Age or Iron Age field systems.

The earliest phase of Stonehenge, a circular earth bank and ditch, has been dated to about 3100 BC. Deposits containing human bone date from as early as 3000 BC, when the ditch and bank were first dug, and continued for at least another 500 years. In 2013, archaeologists excavated more than 50,000 cremated bone fragments from 63 individuals buried at Stonehenge. The cremated were almost equally men and women and included some children.

A jadeitite axehead found beside the Sweet Track in 1973 was probably placed there as an offering, around 3200 BC. Its material came from the Alpine area, and such axe heads in Great Britain are thought to have been non-utilitarian. They may have represented some form of currency or been products of gift exchange.

Most chambered tombs in the British Isles appear to have been built between 4000 and 3200 BC. The archaeologist Mike Parker Pearson notes that this made tomb building "a relatively short-lived fashion in archaeological terms". Disputed dates suggest the Carrowmore tomb in Ireland may be as old as circa 5000 BCE.

The Post Track, dated to around 3838 BCE, is about 30 years older than the Sweet Track. It was likely intended as a permanent fixture, updated, maintained and eventually replaced as it succumbed to the elements. Some of its planks were reused when the Sweet Track was built.

culture.text: After the last Ice Age ended around 9000 BC, England's Mesolithic societies grew increasingly complex. Evidence suggests they may have selectively burned the woodland that covered the land. This would have created clearings where herds gathered and could be hunted.

Many Neolithic groups in Europe lived in small family-based communities. They lived on domestic plants and animals, supplemented by wild plant foods and hunting. They made pottery by hand, without the potter's wheel.

Rising seas submerged Doggerland and cut Britain off from the European mainland for the last time by around 6500 BCE. One account says that with this separation, the Mesolithic in Britain "goes its own way" in cultural terms.

As the climate warmed, Britain's open landscape gave way to pine, birch and alder forest, and reindeer and wild horse herds became scarce. People's diets shifted to pig, elk, red deer, roe deer, wild boar and aurochs. These less social animals required different hunting techniques.
Mesolithic hunters in England used simple projectile weapons, mainly the javelin and possibly the sling. The bow and arrow was already known in Western Europe since at least 9000 BC.
Archaeological sites from the French Neolithic include artefacts of the Linear Pottery culture, dated about 5500 to 4500 BC. They also include the Rössen culture, dated about 4500 to 4000 BC.

The Neolithic way of life spread from the Aegean to Britain over about 2,500 years, between 6500 and 4000 BC. Neolithic peoples in Europe are sometimes called Pre-Indo-Europeans or Old Europe, though archaeologists disagree about when Indo-European languages arrived.
